tests.name: Numerical Reasoning Test 4
tests.subtitle: AssessmentDay source test
tests.description: A 30-question mixed numerical reasoning test based on business tables and charts.
tests.instructions:
This numerical reasoning test comprises 30 questions, and you will have 30 minutes in which to correctly answer as many as you can. Calculators are permitted for this test, and it is recommended you have some rough paper to work on.

You will have to work quickly and accurately to perform well in this test. If you don't know the answer to a question, leave it and come back to it if you have time. Each question will have five possible answers, one of which is correct. You may click Back and Next during the test to review or skip questions.

You can submit your test at any time. If the time limit is up before you click submit the test will automatically be submitted with the answers you have selected. It is recommended to keep working until the time limit is up.

Try to find a time and place where you will not be interrupted during the test. The test will begin on the next page.

questions.prompt: In which year was there the highest ratio of average sales price: average production cost?
What were the total production costs for 2009 (to the nearest £100,000)?
questions.explanation: Total production cost = 12,636 cars × £15,800 = £199,648,800, which rounds to £199.6 million to the nearest £100,000.

questions.prompt: If the dealer paid upfront for the annual service charge of each car sold, in which year would this have cost the dealer the least amount?
If the average sales price for 2010 was 5% higher, but the number of cars sold that year was 9% lower, by what percent would the sales revenue have decreased for 2010?
questions.explanation: Revenue changes by the combined factor 1.05 × 0.91 = 0.9555. The decrease is 1 − 0.9555 = 0.0445 = 4.45%.

questions.prompt: In 2008, car sales were split across 3 equally-priced models in the ratio of 7:8:6 for models A, B and C respectively. What was the sales revenue for model A?
questions.explanation: The ratio has 7 + 8 + 6 = 21 parts. Model A receives 7/21 of £1,005.0 million: £1,005.0 million × 7/21 = £335 million.

questions.sectionTitle: YLF plc – Total costs by year (£000s)
questions.prompt: For how many years has the combined cost of Property depreciation and Staff costs exceeded that of Other expenses?
questions.explanation: Staff plus property is 346 vs 336 in 2006 (exceeds), 351 vs 459 in 2007, 360 vs 357 in 2008 (exceeds), 345 vs 413 in 2009, and 347 vs 502 in 2010. It exceeds Other expenses in 2 years.

questions.sectionTitle: YLF plc – Total costs by year (£000s)
questions.prompt: In which year, or years, was there a 2:1 ratio of Staff costs: Property depreciation?
questions.explanation: A 2:1 ratio requires staff costs to equal twice property depreciation. This holds in 2007 (234 = 2 × 117) and 2009 (230 = 2 × 115), and in no other year.

questions.sectionTitle: YLF plc – Total costs by year (£000s)
questions.prompt: What percent of total costs did Property depreciation represent in 2007?
questions.explanation: Total 2007 costs = 234 + 117 + 12,505 + 12 + 459 = 13,327 (£000s). Property depreciation is 117 ÷ 13,327 × 100 = 0.878%, which rounds to 0.9%.

questions.sectionTitle: YLF plc – Total costs by year (£000s)
questions.prompt: Which cost changed by the second largest percent from 2008 to 2010?
questions.explanation: Absolute percentage changes from 2008 to 2010 are: Other expenses 145/357 = 40.6%; Staff costs 33/248 = 13.3%; Loan impairment 13/9 = 144.4%; Inventories 4,578/11,842 = 38.7%; Property depreciation 20/112 = 17.9%. The second largest is Other expenses.

questions.sectionTitle: YLF plc – Total costs by year (£000s)
questions.prompt: If the 2006 Inventories cost had increased by an eighth compared to the previous year, what was the previous year’s Inventories cost (to the nearest £10,000)?
questions.explanation: An increase by one eighth gives a factor of 1.125. The previous cost was £11.410 million ÷ 1.125 = £10.1422 million, which rounds to £10.14 million to the nearest £10,000.

questions.prompt: Between 2010 and 2011 what is the total cut in the marketing budget across the 5 Brands combined (in €10,000s)?
Which Brand has suffered the largest percentage cut in its Marketing Budget?
Between 2010 and 2011 what has been the mean percentage Budget reduction for each of the 5 Brands (to 1 decimal place)?
questions.explanation: The five percentage reductions are 25.0%, 32.9268%, 32.6923%, 30.0%, and 31.5068%. Their mean is 152.1259% ÷ 5 = 30.4252%, which rounds to 30.4%.

questions.prompt: Brand A and Brand D are to have their number of staff reduced by the same percentage reduction seen by their Marketing Budgets between 2010 and 2011. If the number of staff at Brand A was originally 120 and the number of staff at Brand D triple this, what are the new reduced staff numbers for each Brand?
questions.explanation: Brand A’s budget fell 25%, so 120 × 0.75 = 90 staff. Brand D’s budget fell 30%; its original staff was 3 × 120 = 360, so 360 × 0.70 = 252 staff.

questions.prompt: The total 2011 Marketing Budget for all five Brands is to be cut by a quarter in 2012. In £, what is the 2012 Marketing Budget? (to the nearest £100,000)?
Which terminal had the highest number of passengers per week in Year 2?
questions.explanation: Year 1 totals (thousands) are A 105.6, B 133.1, C 126.0, D 154.0, E 157.3. Applying Year 2 changes gives A 104.016, B 136.428, C 127.890, D 157.080, E 154.154. Terminal D is highest.

questions.prompt: For Year 1 what was the average weekly difference between male and female passengers per terminal?
questions.explanation: Male passengers total 338.3 thousand and female passengers total 337.7 thousand, a difference of 0.6 thousand. Across 5 terminals, 0.6 ÷ 5 = 0.12 thousand = 120 more males per terminal.

questions.prompt: Terminals A and D serve domestic flights, whilst Terminals B, C and E serve international flights. Each week on average how many more passengers in Year 1 took international flights compared to domestic flights (to the nearest 10,000)?
questions.explanation: International passengers = B 133.1 + C 126.0 + E 157.3 = 416.4 thousand. Domestic passengers = A 105.6 + D 154.0 = 259.6 thousand. Difference = 156.8 thousand, which rounds to 160,000.

questions.prompt: In Year 2 each passenger spends on average £4.25 in Terminal C’s shops. How much is the average weekly revenue for Terminal C’s shops in Year 2 (to the nearest £10,000)?
questions.explanation: Terminal C had 62.9 + 63.1 = 126.0 thousand passengers in Year 1. Year 2 has 126,000 × 1.015 = 127,890 passengers. Revenue = 127,890 × £4.25 = £543,532.50, which rounds to £540,000.

questions.prompt: A competitor airport operator called Vefy Flights operates a different airport with half the average Year 1 weekly number of passengers operating from 3 terminals. What is Vefy Flights’s average weekly number of passengers per terminal (to the nearest 1,000)?
questions.explanation: The five terminals total 676.0 thousand Year 1 passengers. Half is 338.0 thousand; across 3 competitor terminals, 338.0 ÷ 3 = 112.667 thousand, which rounds to 113,000.

questions.prompt: If the total 2010 costs represent a 5% increase on the total 2009 costs, what were the total 2009 costs (to the nearest £million)?
questions.explanation: The 2010 quarterly table totals 3,853 units of £10,000 = £38.53 million. Reversing a 5% increase gives £38.53m ÷ 1.05 = £36.695m, which rounds to £37 million.

questions.prompt: Which cost or costs on their own represented more than 17% of the total costs in 2010?
options: Supply chain, Labour, Production and I.T.
questions.explanation: The 2010 total is 3,853, so 17% is 655.01. Annual category totals are Overheads 412, Supply chain 688, Labour 1,077, I.T. 618, and Production 1,058. Supply chain, Labour, and Production each exceed 655.01.

questions.prompt: In which of the years shown was there a 3:2 ratio of IT to Overheads costs?
If 2009’s total costs were £250,000, what were the Production costs?
If the costs are put into order of decreasing size, in which two years is the order the same?
questions.explanation: In 2006 the order is Labour > Production > Supply chain > I.T. > Overheads. The 2010 totals are Labour 1,077 > Production 1,058 > Supply chain 688 > I.T. 618 > Overheads 412, the same order. The other listed pairs differ.

questions.prompt: On average, families from which country of origin spend the most during a typical stay?
questions.explanation: Typical family spend is days × daily spend: Australia £1,227.20; Spain £324.80; Germany £680.80; U.S.A. £1,512.80; Italy £623.20. U.S.A. is highest.

questions.prompt: On average, families from which of the countries shown spend the most and the least per typical stay?
questions.explanation: Typical family spends are Australia £1,227.20, Spain £324.80, Germany £680.80, U.S.A. £1,512.80, and Italy £623.20. U.S.A. is most and Spain is least.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is True?
options: The ratio of German:Spanish tourists is 1:2
There are fewer Spanish tourists than German and Italian tourists combined
German families have the longest average length of stay
Total German tourist spending is more than 92% of Total Spanish tourist spending
There are over 4 times as many Australian tourists as Italian tourists
questions.explanation: 92% of Spanish spending is 0.92 × £410m = £377.2m; German spending is £380m, which is greater. The other statements fail: 660:1,300 is not exactly 1:2; 1,300 > 660+550; U.S.A. has the longest stay; and 2,200 is exactly, not over, four times 550.

questions.prompt: On average which of the following tour parties would spend the most per day?
questions.explanation: Daily party spends are 2×£236 = £472; 2×£116 = £232; 3×£148 = £444; 3×£244 = £732; and 3×£164 = £492. Three U.S.A. families spend the most.

questions.prompt: Approximately, what’s the average daily spend per family for the 5 countries of origin shown?
questions.explanation: The five displayed figures are averages for each country, but the number of families from each country is not provided. A simple mean would incorrectly give each country equal weight, so the overall average daily spend per family cannot be determined from the data.

questions.prompt: What was the unit sales ratio of Austrian Quarter 4 : Portugal Quarter 1: Greek Quarter 4?
questions.explanation: The values are 35,000 : 28,000 : 21,000. Dividing all three by 7,000 gives 5:4:3.

questions.prompt: Which country met or exceeded its annual target for unit sales?
questions.explanation: Annual totals versus targets are Greece 108,300 vs 110,000; Portugal 104,200 vs 105,000; Austria 105,800 vs 105,000; Ireland 102,400 vs 105,000; Croatia 105,200 vs 110,000. Only Austria meets or exceeds target.

questions.prompt: The previous year’s average number of Portuguese units sold per quarter was 20% higher than the year shown. What was the previous year’s average number of Portuguese units sold per quarter?

If Austria’s annual corporation tax was 22% on the first €200,000 of sales and 20% on sales exceeding €200,000, how much is their corporation tax bill for the year (assuming each unit is sold at €3.5)?
Greek and Irish sales generated 2.5 Euros per unit sold, whilst the other countries’ sales generated 2.25 Euros per unit sold. Which country or countries exceeded their Annual Product Sales Target?
questions.explanation: Revenues are Greece 108,300×€2.5 = €270,750 (above €250,000); Portugal €234,450 (below €240,000); Austria €238,050 (below €240,000); Ireland €256,000 (below €260,000); Croatia €236,700 (above €230,000). Greece and Croatia exceed target.

questions.prompt: Which shares have increased and decreased respectively in value by the largest percent from yesterday to today?
questions.explanation: Percentage changes are A +0.6/19.4 = +3.09%, B +0.3/3.9 = +7.69%, C −1.2/19.3 = −6.22%, D +0.5/5.1 = +9.80%, E −0.2/3.3 = −6.06%. D increased most and C decreased most.

questions.prompt: A dealer buys 250 Share Ds and 350 Share Es at yesterday’s prices and sells these at today’s prices. How much profit or loss does the dealer make?
questions.explanation: Share D profit is 250 × (£5.6−£5.1) = £125. Share E loss is 350 × (£3.1−£3.3) = −£70. Net result = £125−£70 = £55 profit.

questions.prompt: A trader has 200,000 Share Bs to sell at today’s price and today plans to split her proceeds equally into an investment in Share A and Share D. In how many Share As and Share Ds does the trader invest?
questions.explanation: Selling 200,000 Share Bs yields 200,000×£4.2 = £840,000. Each investment receives £420,000. This buys £420,000/£20 = 21,000 Share As and £420,000/£5.6 = 75,000 Share Ds.

questions.prompt: What was the total cost of buying 550 Share C’s yesterday and 1,050 Share E’s today (to the nearest $1,000)?
questions.explanation: Yesterday’s Share C purchase cost 550×£19.3 = £10,615, converted at $1.63/£ = $17,302.45. Today’s Share E purchase cost 1,050×£3.1 = £3,255, converted at $1.62/£ = $5,273.10. Total = $22,575.55, which rounds to $23,000.

questions.prompt: Today’s prices for Share A and Share C (in Euros) respectively represent a 15% decrease and a 22% increase on the price (in Euros) one year ago. What were the respective prices a year ago (to the nearest Euro)?

questions.sectionTitle: Year 2 Product Sales by UK region
questions.prompt: Which two products had the same total product sales in Year 2?
questions.explanation: Totals in chart units are A 22.5, B 27.5, C 23.5, and D 27.5. Products B and D have the same total.

questions.sectionTitle: Year 2 Product Sales by UK region
questions.prompt: As a percentage of total sales across all regions, how has the Eastern region’s sales changed between Year 1 and Year 2?
questions.explanation: Year 2 Eastern sales total 4.5+5.5+5.5+5.0 = 20.5, while all Year 2 regions total 101. Eastern’s Year 2 share is 20.5/101×100 = 20.30%. Compared with its Year 1 share of 22%, this is 1.70 percentage points less.

questions.sectionTitle: Year 2 Product Sales by UK region
questions.prompt: For products A, B, C and D combined, which region had a sales value different from the other regions in Year 2?
questions.explanation: Regional totals are Northern 20.5, Southern 20.5, Eastern 20.5, Western 20.5, and Central 19.0. Central is the only different value.

questions.sectionTitle: Year 2 Product Sales by UK region
questions.prompt: The 5 regions shown represent UK product sales, which is one-quarter of the value of US product sales and 50% of the value of Asian product sales. What are Year 2’s total product sales for all 3 territories combined?
questions.explanation: UK sales total 101×£10,000 = £1.01 million. US sales are 4×UK = £4.04 million, and Asian sales are 2×UK = £2.02 million. Combined = £1.01m+£4.04m+£2.02m = £7.07 million.

questions.sectionTitle: Year 2 Product Sales by UK region
questions.prompt: Which region experienced the greatest change in its share of total UK sales between Year 1 and Year 2?
questions.explanation: Year 2 shares from the chart are Northern, Southern, Eastern, and Western each 20.5/101 = 20.30%, and Central 19/101 = 18.81%. Absolute changes from Year 1 are 1.70, 3.70, 1.70, 2.30, and 4.81 percentage points respectively. Central changed most.

questions.prompt: Next year, which liability is projected to have experienced the second highest percentage change in value compared with last year?
questions.explanation: Absolute changes from previous year to next year are current interest loans 0.74%, currency swaps 18.82%, other current liabilities 15.0%, non-current interest-bearing loans 19.62%, pension payments 6.86%, and tax liabilities 3.13%. Currency swaps have the second highest change.

questions.prompt: What is the average difference between the total Non-Current Liabilities and the total Current Liabilities for the 3 years shown (to the nearest £million)?

If the projected figures shown prove accurate and the same percentage changes occur for each liability in the year after next, what will the total Current Liabilities be in the year after next (to the nearest £million)?
questions.explanation: Repeat each current-to-next factor: interest loans 134×(134/126) = 142.54; currency swaps 6.9×(6.9/11.3) = 4.21; other current liabilities 48.3×(48.3/52) = 44.86. Total = £191.61m, which rounds to £192m.

questions.prompt: The Pension payments figure for each year is based upon the following numbers of ex-employees drawing a pension: 8,155 (previous year); 8,240 (current year); 8,325 (next year). What is the average pension payable across the 3 years shown (to the nearest £1,000)?
questions.explanation: Per-person pensions are £204m/8,155 = £25,015; £196m/8,240 = £23,786; and £218m/8,325 = £26,186. Their mean is about £24,996, which rounds to £25,000.

questions.prompt: Next year’s projected figures need to be corrected by adding an additional 4% for inflation. What is next year’s corrected total Non-Current Liabilities?
questions.explanation: Next year’s Non-Current Liabilities total £42.6m+£218m+£49.5m = £310.1m. Adding 4% gives £310.1m×1.04 = £322.504m, shown as £322.5 million.

questions.prompt: What was the global income for Ploche Inc in 2007 (to the nearest £10,000)?
questions.explanation: Ploche’s 2006 income was (13.5+11.6+13.9+15.3)×£100,000 = £5.43m. Applying 2007 growth of 1.4% gives £5.43m×1.014 = £5.50602m, which rounds to £5.51m.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true?
options: Ploche Inc increased global income each quarter during 2006
Between 2007-2010 Zwex Ltd has experienced 6.9% global income growth
In 2006 Quew plc’s global income was £5,430,000
Ploche Inc has experienced positive global growth each year between 2006-2010
The average 2006 Quarter 2 sales were £1.15 million
questions.explanation: Ploche’s annual growth rates for 2007–2010 are 1.4%, 1.2%, 1.6%, and 0.5%, all positive, so D is true. A is false because Quarter 2 fell; C is false because Quew totals £5.41m; E is false because the Quarter 2 company mean is £1.273m; and B’s 6.9% is only the sum of rates, not compounded growth.

questions.prompt: In which year up to 2010 did Quew plc experience a higher annual % growth than either Zwex Ltd or Ploche Inc?
questions.explanation: Quew’s growth is below both competitors in 2007, 2008, and 2009. In 2010 Quew grew 1.1%, which is higher than Ploche’s 0.5% (though lower than Zwex’s 1.8%), so 2010 is the year it exceeded either named competitor.

questions.prompt: In 2006 Zwex’s Global sales comprised European and non-European sales, which were in the ratio 3:4. What were Zwex’s European sales for 2006?
What was the global income for Quew plc in 2008 (to the nearest £100,000)?
From 2006 to 2007 Attributable profit increased at double the percentage rate as it did between 2005-2006. What was the Attributable profit figure for 2005?
questions.explanation: The 2006–2007 increase rate is (£2.11m−£1.95m)/£1.95m = 8.205%. The 2005–2006 rate was half, 4.103%. Therefore 2005 profit = £1.95m/1.04103 = £1.873m, or £1.87 million.

questions.prompt: If the target was to have an average profit (per unit) in excess of 50p, in which year or years was this achieved?
questions.explanation: Divide profit per 500 units by 500: 2006 = 50p, 2007 = 65p, 2008 = 35p, 2009 = 40p, 2010 = 60p. “In excess of 50p” excludes 2006, leaving 2007 and 2010.

questions.prompt: In 2011, if Adjusted earnings increase by an eighth and there is a 2:3 ratio of (2011 Adjusted earnings: 2011 Cash flow), what will be the Cash flow in 2011?
questions.explanation: 2011 adjusted earnings = £1.11m×(1+1/8) = £1.24875m. With adjusted earnings:cash flow = 2:3, cash flow = £1.24875m×3/2 = £1.873125m, or £1.87 million.

questions.prompt: Which year had the lowest ratio of Adjusted earnings to Attributable profit?
Which year from 2007 onwards showed the greatest percentage change in Cash flow compared to the preceding year?
